parole.significato: a French person, or a person of French descent
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch fransois, from Old French François. The meaning of “Frenchman (derogatory)” was first attested in 1240.
From Middle Dutch fraude, from Old French fraude, a borrowing from Latin fraus, fraudem.
From Middle Dutch furet, fret, from Old French furet, from Vulgar Latin *fūrittus, diminutive of Latin fūr (“thief”).
From Middle Dutch fronsen, from Old French froncer.
From Old French front (noun), fronter (verb), from Latin frons (“forehead”).

parole.significato: fruit (produced by trees or bushes, or any sweet vegetable; only literal sense)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch fruut, froyt, from Old French fruit, from Latin frūctus. Doublet of vrucht.

parole.significato: to fry in boiling fat (now chiefly of culinary vegetables in small volumes of fat)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch fruten, older friten (“to fry”), from Old French frit, past participle of frire (“to fry”). Folk-etymologically influenced by fruit.
From Middle Dutch fondament, from Old French fundement, fondement, from Latin fundāmentum (“foundation”), from fundō (“to lay the bottom, to found”).

From earlier fuste (“type of wine barrel”), from Middle Dutch fuust (“barrel”), borrowed from Old French fust (“wine barrel, piece of wood”), from Latin fusta, fustum (“block of wood, barrel”), from earlier fustis (“cludgel”). Cognate with English fust.

parole.significato: jaybird (Garrulus glandarius), a woodland corvine species
parole.testo: From Old French gai, from Late Latin gaius (“jay”). Further etymology uncertain, though plausibly echoic, and supposedly influenced by the Roman common given name Gaius. Doublet of gay and gei.
From Middle Dutch galiote, from Old French galiot.
From Middle Dutch goreel, from Old French gorel.
Inherited from Middle Dutch gay, gaey, derived from Old French gai. Doublet of gaai and gay.
From Middle Dutch geometrie, from Old French geometrie, from Latin geōmetria, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρία (geōmetría).
From Middle Dutch gescakiert (“checkered, chequy”), from Old French eschequeré.

From Middle Dutch geule, from two possible origins (which may have merged): * from Old French goule (“mouth”), and/or * from Old Dutch *gulja (as in the hydronym Geul, attested in 10th-century Latin as Gulia), of Proto-Germanic origin; perhaps cognate with Swedish göl.
From Middle Dutch genst, from Old French geneste, from Latin genista. Cognate with German Ginster.

parole.significato: curtain (piece of cloth covering a window)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gordine, gardine, from Old French cortine, from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”).
From Middle Dutch grael, from Old French graal, greal (“cup”), from Medieval Latin gradalis, possibly corrupted over time from Latin crater (“bowl”).
From Middle Dutch gracioos, from Old French gracieus, from Latin grātiōsus.

parole.significato: a grenade; e.g. a hand grenade, an artillery shell
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch garnate, grenate, from Old French grenat, from Latin pomus granatus (“seeded apple”).

From Middle Dutch garnate-appel, also in phrases like appelen van gernaten. A partial calque of Old French pume grenate, also found as simply grenate. By surface analysis, granaat + appel. See granaat for more.
From Middle Dutch graveren, from Old French graver, from Frankish *graban, from Proto-Germanic *grabaną. Doublet of graven.

parole.significato: grievance, complaint, bone to pick, issue
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch grief, from Old French grief, from Early Medieval Latin grevem, alteration of Latin gravem.
From Middle Dutch gros, from Old French gros, from Latin grossus; gross sense probably directly from French.
From Middle Dutch gruus, from Old French groisse, a Germanic borrowing, from Frankish *greot, ultimately related to *greutą (“grits, coarse grains”).

parole.significato: gruel, especially made with barley grits, usually sweetened with berry juice
parole.testo: Ultimately from Old French gruel.

parole.significato: eating excessively quickly and/or too much, very keen to eat, gluttonous
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gulsich, from guls + -ich, with guls probably from Old French golos, possibly influenced by Latin gulōsus.
From Middle Dutch haest, from Northern Old French haste. Compare with German fast.

parole.significato: habit (dress worn by monks and nuns)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch habijt, from Old French habit, from Latin habitus.
From Middle Dutch harmonia, armonie, from Old French harmonie, from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía).

parole.significato: harpy (hybrid of a woman and a bird of prey)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch harpie, arpie, from Old French harpie, from Latin harpyia, from Ancient Greek ἅρπυια (hárpuia).

parole.significato: a harpoon, short spearlike weapon with a barbed head thrown at the target, of various sizes and types, e.g. used for wh…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch arpoen, from Old French harpon (“hook, hold-on”). Cognate with English harpoon, German Harpune.

From southern Middle Dutch her- (“re-, again”). Of uncertain origin, but mostly considered a borrowing from Old French re- or specifically its northern variant er-, from Latin re- (existing as a doublet in the borrowed prefix re-). In certain contexts this prefix touched on the native Middle Dutch h

From Middle Dutch heraut, from Old French heraut, from Frankish *heriwald, from Proto-Germanic *harjawaldaz, a compound consisting of *ker- (“army”) + *h₂welh₁- (“to be strong, to rule”), equivalent to modern Dutch heer (“army”) + weld (“power, authority”). Compare Wouter, which has these elements r
From Middle Dutch herberghier, probably adapted from Old French herbergier (compare modern French héberger), as hinted by the suffix.
From Middle Dutch hermitage, from Old French ermitage, from Latin heremitagium.
From Old French ierarchie, from Latin hierarchia, from Ancient Greek ἱεραρχία (hierarkhía, “rule of a high priest”).
From Middle Dutch orlogie, from Old French orloge, from Latin hōrologium, from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion). The current spelling was influenced by Modern French horloge.

parole.significato: hospital, now in particular a military hospital
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hospitael, Old French hospital (Modern French hôpital), from Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”), from hospes (“host, guest”).
Borrowed from Old French hoel or hael, diminutive from hoe (“hoe, mattock”), which is itself derived from Old Dutch houwan (“to hew”).

From Middle Dutch hoyke, huuc, huke, from Old Dutch heucken, probably borrowed from Old French huque, heuque, from Medieval Latin hapax huca, of uncertain origin, possibly ultimately related to huig (“uvula”).
From Middle Dutch humuere, from Old French humor, humour, from Latin hūmor. Doublet of humor.

parole.significato: an idol, a statue or image that is the subject of worship
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ydool, from Old French idole, from Latin idolum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”).
From Old French ignorance.

parole.significato: prepended to an adjective to negate its meaning; occurs mostly in borrowed terms from French: in-, un-
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch in-, which is borrowed from Old French in- and Latin in-.
From Middle Dutch institute, from Old French [Term?], from Latin īnstitūtum.
From Middle Dutch instrument, from Old French instrument, from Latin īnstrūmentum.
From Old French intelligence, from Latin intelligentia.
From Middle Dutch intencie, from Old French entencion, from Latin intentiō.

From interpreteren + -atie; from Old French, from Latin interpretationem, accusative of interpretatio, noun of action from interpretari (“to explain, expound, interpret, understand, conclude, infer, comprehend”).
From inunderen + -atie; from Old French inundacion (“flood”) (French inondation), from Latin inundatio (“a flood”), form of inundō (“to flood, overflow”) (English inundate).

parole.significato: ivory, a hard natural material from elephant tusks and some other mammals' teeth
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ivore, ivorie, from Old French ivorie, from Latin eboreus, from ebur (“ivory”), from Demotic Egyptian yb (“ivory, Elephantine”), from Egyptian ꜣbw (“elephant, ivory, Elephantine”).
From Middle Dutch jak, borrowed from Old French jaque (“medieval doublet”). Cognate with English jacket.

From Middle Dutch jalours, jaloers, also jalous, jaloes, from Old French jalous, from Late Latin zelosus. The -r- is not etymological and does not appear in any other language; even the related Dutch term jaloezie lacks it. Its origin is unknown, but may have arisen by analogy if the endings -s and
From Middle Dutch jalosie, from Old French jalosie, from jalous.
From Old French jargon (“chatter, talk, language”).

From Middle Dutch jegenode, from jegen (“against”) + -ode, literally “the land which lies opposed to the observer”. Originally a calque of Old French contrée, from Vulgar Latin (terra) contrāta (“opposite land”). Cognate to German Gegend.
From Middle Dutch jenever, genever, geniver, from Old French genevre, from Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus (“juniper”).
From Middle Dutch iolijd, borrowed from Old French joli, with influence from synonymous Middle Dutch delijt.
From Middle Dutch juust, from Old French juste, from Latin iūstus, from Proto-Italic *jowestos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-. More at just.

Uncertain. Possibly shortened from earlier *jurreken (compare English jerkin), assimilated from *jurneken, from Middle Dutch jo(u)rney, journede (“surcoat”), from Old French journée, formed from jor (“day (of the tournament)”), with the suffix -ade (“at, from or before”). In the sense 'clothing' fir

parole.significato: to card (to use a carding device to disentangle the fibres of wool prior to spinning)
parole.testo: From Old French carde, from Old Occitan carda, deverbal from carder, from Late Latin caritare, from Latin carrere (“to comb with a card”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). By surface analysis, kaarde + -en.
From Middle Dutch cāerte, from Old French carte, from Latin charta.
Shortening of kaffetorie, from Old French covertoir, from Latin coopertorium.

From Middle Dutch kayhute, of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly borrowed from Old French. According to Watkins, possibly a mix of cabane + hutte. Cognate with German Kajüte (from Middle Low German kajüte), French cahute.
From Middle Dutch kalendier, from Old French calendier, from Latin calendārium. The form ending on -er was influenced by German Kalender.
From Middle Dutch cameleon, from Old French cameleon, from Latin chamaeleōn, from Ancient Greek χαμαιλέων (khamailéōn), ultimately a calque of Akkadian 𒌨𒈤𒊭𒆠.
From Old French chan, from Medieval Latin canus, caanus, of Turkic origin, from Old Turkic xān (“Central Asian khan”), probably ultimately of non-Turkic (Central Asian) origin.

From Middle Dutch canael, from older canel, from Old French canal, from Latin canālis (“pipe, channel, canal”), from canna (“reed, cane”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”), from Sumerian 𒄀𒈾 (gi.na).

parole.significato: rock sugar or rock candy (crystalline sugar confectionery)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch candi, candijt (“rock sugar”), from Old French candi (“candied”), from Arabic قَنْدِي (qandī), genitive of قَنْد (qand, “rock sugar”), from Persian کند (kand, “candied sugar”) from Sanskrit खण्ड (khaṇḍa, “candied sugar”).
From Middle Dutch caneel, from Old French canele, a diminutive that ultimately derives from Latin canna (“reed”).

parole.significato: something or someone who is big or the biggest of their kind; a whopper
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch keniart, canjaert, kangart, kenjard, from Old French cagnard.
From Middle Dutch cantoor, from Old French comtoir.

parole.significato: captain (person in command of a ship)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch capitein, from Old French capitaine, from Medieval Latin capitāneus.
From Middle Dutch cardemome, cardamome, from Old French cardamome, from Latin cardamomum, from Ancient Greek καρδάμωμον (kardámōmon).
From Middle Dutch corweide, from Old French corvee, from Late Latin conrogāta. Doublet of corvee.

parole.significato: cotton, plant of the genus Gossypium
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch catoen, from older cotoen, from Old French coton, from Old Italian cotone, from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun).
From Middle Dutch cajacke, from Old French casaque. The form with j was displaced under influence of Middle French and French casaque.
From Middle Dutch ketsen, borrowed from Old French cachier. Doublet of kaatsen.

parole.significato: a khan (Turkic, Tatar or Mongolic ruler)
parole.testo: From Old French chan, from Medieval Latin canus, caanus, of Turkic origin, from Old Turkic xān (“Central Asian khan”), probably ultimately of non-Turkic (Central Asian) origin.
From kokeloer, kokerol (“snail”), from Old French coque (“large hollow shell”).
From Middle Dutch cofer, couer, from Old French cofre, coffre, from Latin cophinus (“basket”), from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “basket”).

parole.significato: a medieval piece of leather armour covering the torso
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kolre, koller, from Old French coler, from Latin collāre. Closely related to collier, which deriving instead from collārium is not an exact doublet.

From Middle Dutch colomme, from Old French columne, from Latin columna (“a column, pillar, post”), originally a collateral form of columen, contraction culmen (“a pillar, top, crown, summit”). Doublet of column and colonne.
From Middle Dutch comete, from Old French comete, from Latin comēta, from Ancient Greek κομήτης (komḗtēs).
From Middle Dutch cucumer, from Old French concombre, from Latin cucumis.
From Middle Dutch compas (“circle, pair of compasses, compass”), from Old French compas.

parole.significato: a rabbit, a bunny; any non-hare lagomorph of the family Leporidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch conijn, from earlier Middle Dutch conin, from Old French connin, a variant of Old French conil, from Latin cunīculus, perhaps from Iberian or Celtiberian. Cognate to English cony, German Kaninchen, Spanish conejo and Portuguese coelho.

parole.significato: a rope, cord (length of twisted strands)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch corde, coorde, from Old French corde, from Latin chorda, from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, the string of a lyre”). Doublet of koorde.
From Middle Dutch copie, from Old French copie, from Latin copia.
From Middle Dutch coppel, from Old French cople. Doublet of copula.
From Middle Dutch coppelen, which is likely denominative from coppel (modern koppel) and/or directly from Old French cupler. By surface analysis, koppel (“couple”) + -en.

parole.significato: coral (any of various coralline tiny organisms of the class Anthozoa, notably of genus Corallium, who live in marine co…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch corael, from Old French coral, from Latin corallium, from Ancient Greek κοράλλιον (korállion); see coral for more.
From Middle Dutch coriander, from Old French coriandre, from Latin coriandrum, from Ancient Greek κορίανδρον (koríandron), alternative form of κορίαννον (koríannon).
From Middle Dutch cornuut, from Old French cornut, from Latin cornūtus.
From Middle Dutch cost, from Old French cost. Compare German Kost and Kosten (respectively with the same semantic developments).

parole.significato: a churchwarden, a caretaker at a church, sacristan
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch coster, from Old French costre, from Late Latin custor, from custōs.
From Middle Dutch cassijn, from Old French cassin.
From Middle Dutch cosin, from Old French cosin.

parole.significato: a carrack, a nau; a large, 16th/17th century, Iberian type of war - or commercial naval ship
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch crake, from Old French caraque, from Old Spanish carraca, Italian caracca or Medieval Latin carraca, from Latin carrus or Arabic قَرَاقِير (qarāqīr).

parole.significato: a cadaver, carcass, corpse, especially when in a state of decay; in particular an animal corpse
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch krenge, from Old French carogne (“carrion”), cognate of English crone.
From Middle Dutch cristal, kerstal, from Old French cristal, from Latin crystallum, from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos).
From Middle Dutch cristallijn, from Old French cristallin, from Latin crystallinus. Equivalent to kristal + -ijn.
From Middle Dutch croos, from Old French croist, from croistre, from Latin crēscere (“to grow”).
From Middle Dutch cul, kul (“testicle”), from Old French coille, from Latin cōleus (“testicle”).
From Middle Dutch cost, from Old French coste, from Latin costa (“rib, side”), cognate with English coast, German Küste, French côte etc.
From Middle Dutch cure (13th c.), from Old French cure, from Latin cūra.

parole.significato: a quarter, one of four (equal) parts
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch quarte, from Old French quart, from Latin quārta.

parole.significato: a quarter of an hour, i.e. 15 minutes
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch quartier, from Old French quartier, from Latin quartārius.
From Middle Dutch quetsen, from Old Dutch quezzon, of uncertain origin but compare German quetschen. Early influence or even borrowing of the Old Dutch term from Old French quasser has been proposed.
From Middle Dutch quiten, from Old French quiter, from Latin quiētāre.
From Middle Dutch quitantie, from Old French quittance.

parole.significato: a horse-riding set-up with a beam and two shafts, to which a horse harness can be strapped
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch lamoen, from Old French limon.

From Middle Dutch lampe, from Old French lampe, from Latin lampas (“lamp; torch; lantern”), from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “torch; lamp”), from λάμπω (lámpō, “shine”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂p- (“glow”).
Inherited from Middle Dutch lampreel, borrowed from Old French lapriel.
From Middle Dutch lanterne, from Old French lanterne, from Latin lanterna, from Ancient Greek λᾰμπτήρ (lămptḗr).
From an earlier landtrefant, from landtrouwandt (“vagabond”), a compound of land + trouwant (“vagabond, beggar”), from Old French truant (“vagabond, beggar”), whence also trawant and English truant.
From Middle Dutch lasschen (“to join together”). Further etymology is unclear, but probably borrowed from Old French lacer (“to tie”).
From Middle Dutch latuwe, from Old French laitue, from Latin lactūca.
Inherited from Middle Dutch legioen, derived from Old French legion, derived from Latin legiō. Doublet of legio.
From Middle Dutch lettere, from Old French lettre, from Latin littera.
From Middle Dutch leveren, from Old French livrer.
From Old French licence, from Latin licentia (“license”), from licens, present participle of licere (“to be allowed, be allowable”). Compare Latin linquere, Ancient Greek λείπω (leípō, “leave”).
From Middle Dutch limiten, from Old French limite, from Latin līmes.
From Middle Dutch linie, from Old French ligne, from Latin līnea.

parole.significato: a livery, fancy uniform in the employer's house colours, notably in domestic service
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch livereye, from Old French livree.
From Middle Dutch lombart (“pawnshop, pawnbroker; usurer; Lombard”), from Old French lombard, from Italian lombardo. Doublet of Lombard and Langobard.
From Middle Dutch loodse, loge, from Old French loge. Doublet of loge, lodge, and loggia.
From Middle Dutch loyael, from Old French loyal, from Latin lēgālis.
From Middle Dutch lupaert, leupart, liepart, from Old Dutch *liupard, from Old French leopard, from Late Latin leopardus, from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos).
From Middle Dutch litse, from Old French lice, from Vulgar Latin līcia, from Latin līcium.
From Middle Dutch makereel, from Old French maquerel.

parole.significato: mold, cast (device to help creating shapes)
parole.testo: First attested in the seventeenth century. Ultimately derived from Old French molle, by-form of modle, an old (11th century) borrowing from Latin modulus (“measure”). Doublet of module and modulus.
From Old French maille (“loop, stich”), from Latin macula (“blemish, mesh”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *smh₁-tleh₂, from *smeh₁- (“smear, rub”).
From Middle Dutch mandaet, from Old French mandat, from Latin mandātum.
From Middle Dutch mangeneel, from Old French manganel, from Latin manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγανον (mánganon).
Ultimately from Old French mangonel, from Latin manganellus, manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγανον (mánganon).
From Middle Dutch maniere, from Old French maniere.

parole.significato: maniple, ornamental scarf or band worn over the left arm by priests
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch manipele, from Old French maniple, from Latin manipulus.
Inherited from Middle Dutch marge, maerge, from Old French marge, from Latin margō.
From Middle Dutch marchijs, from Old French marquis, from Italian marchese.
From Middle Dutch masse, from Old French masse, from Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza). The Latin spelling was adopted in the seventeenth century.
From Middle Dutch mat (“checkmate”), borrowed from Old French mat, borrowed from Persian شاه مات (šâh mât, “the king is dead”). Cognate to English checkmate.
From Middle Dutch mat, borrowed from Old French mat, from Latin mattus (“depressed”). See also French mat (adjective).
From Middle Dutch materie, from Old French materie, matiere, from Latin māteria (“matter, stuff, material”).

parole.significato: a mattress (a firm pad on which a person can recline and sleep)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch matrasse, matratse, from Old French materas (modern matelas), from Italian materasso (cognate with Occitan almatrac, Spanish almadraque, Portuguese almadraque), from Arabic مَطْرَح (maṭraḥ), itself perhaps from مُطْرَح (muṭraḥ).
From Middle Dutch matrijs, borrowed from Old French matrice, from Latin mātrīcem, accusative of mātrīx.

From Old French mecanique, from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines or mechanics, inventive”), from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines or contrivance, mechanic, ingenious, inventive”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, contrivance”); see machine.

From Middle Dutch malaetsch, extended form (with the suffix -s) of Middle Dutch malate, malade (“leprous”), itself from Old French malade (“ill, sick”). The specific use for “leprous” may already have existed in French, cf. Middle French grosse maladie (“leprosy”). See also Melaten, a medieval lepro

parole.significato: melody (sequence of notes that makes up a major musical phrase)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch melodie, from Old French melodie, from Latin melōdia.
From Old French marle from Late Latin margila, diminutive of marga (“marl”).

From Old French metal (“metal”), from Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”), from μέταλλευειν (métalleuein, “to mine, quarry”), of unknown origin, but apparently related to μέταλλαν (métallan, “to seek after”), also of unknown
From Middle Dutch meubel, from Old French meuble, from Latin rēs mōbilis (“movable object”). Doublet of mobiel.

parole.significato: mine (place where ore is taken out of the ground)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mine, from Old French mine, from Late Latin mina, from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *meinis (“ore, metal”). Some senses are borrowed from French mine (“explosive device”) and Middle French mine (“tunnel for sapping”).

parole.significato: mitre (headgear worn on solemn occasions by church dignitaries)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mitre, mitere, miter, from Old French mitre, from Latin mītra, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra).

parole.significato: to sap, to mine (to undermine the enemy with tunneling and explosives)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mineren, from Old French miner.

From Middle Dutch mirakele, from Old French miracle, from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *smei-, *mei- (“to smile, to be astonished”).
Alteration (by assimilation to moer (“moor”)) of Middle Dutch marasch, from Old French mareis (“marsh”). Doublet of meers.
From Middle Dutch monarchie, from Old French monarchie, from Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχίᾱ (monarkhíā). Equivalent to monarch + -ie.

parole.significato: a monster, terrifying and dangerous creature
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch monster, probably from Old French monstre, from Latin mōnstrum. Cognate with English monster.

parole.significato: a Moor (member of a Berber people from western North Africa, also ruling parts of Spain during the Middle Ages)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch moor, from Old French maure, from Latin Maurus, from Ancient Greek Μαῦρος (Maûros).
From Middle Dutch moriaen, from Old French morien, from Latin mauretanus. Equivalent to Moor + -iaan.

parole.significato: mussel, bivalve of the family Mytilidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mossel, mussel, from Old French moule, mousle, muisle, from Latin mūsculus. Note that Middle Dutch also attests a form mosschele (with various spelling variants), which is not directly ancestral to this Modern Dutch form and which is said to be an older loanword directly from Latin
From Middle Dutch mostaert, from Old French moustarde (French: moutarde), from moust (“must”), from Latin mustum.
From Middle Dutch motijf, from Old French motif, from Latin mōtīvus.
From Middle Dutch muyte, from earlier muyten, borrowed from Old French meute (modern émeute).
From Middle Dutch nacie, from Old French nacion, from Latin nātiō.
From Middle Dutch nature, from Old French nature, from Latin nātūra.
From Middle Dutch net, which is borrowed from Old French net, from Latin nitidus.
From Middle Dutch note, from Old French note, from Latin nota.

parole.significato: a nutmeg (the hard aromatic seed of the Moluccan tree Myristica fragrans)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch notemusscate, from Old French nois muscate, from Latin nux muscata. Equivalent to noot (“nut”) + muskaat (“nutmeg (tree)”).

parole.significato: number used as a means of identification
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nommer, from Old French nombre, from Latin numerus. The shift from masculine gender in Middle Dutch to neuter gender in modern Dutch is potentially due to the influence of its synonyms getal and cijfer which both have the neuter gender.
From Middle Dutch obligacie, from Old French obligation, from Latin obligātiō.
From Old French obscur, from Latin obscūrus (“dark, dusky, indistinct”). Akin to English obscure and German obskur.
From Middle Dutch offerande, from Old French offrande, from Latin offerenda.
From Middle Dutch officier (“official”), from Old French officier, from Latin officiārius.
From Middle Dutch olifant, from Old French olifant, from Latin elephantus, from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās).
From Middle Dutch opinie, from Old French opinion, from Latin opīniō, from opīnor (“to opine”).

From Middle Dutch arance, orange, from Old French orenge, arange, from Italian arancia, from Arabic نَارَنْج (nāranj), from Classical Persian نارنگ (nārang), from Sanskrit नारङ्ग (nāraṅga), from Dravidian. The spelling was subsequently influenced by Middle French orange.
From Middle Dutch ordene, from Old French ordene, from Latin ordō, ordinem.

parole.significato: to bring into order, to tidy
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ordenen, borrowed, partly via Old French ordene (modern French ordre), from Latin ōrdo (“series, row, order”). Related to English order.

The sense "to coax, sweet-talk" is inherited from Middle Dutch payen, which derives from Old French paiier (“to pay; to satisfy”). The sense "to spawn" is probably etymologically identical, but the details are uncertain.

parole.motivo_incerta: Possibly; Probably; ipotesi scartata nel testo
parole.significato: page (boy serving a knight or noble, often of the noble estate)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch page, from Old French page, possibly via Italian paggio, from Late Latin pagius (“servant”), probably from Ancient Greek παιδίον (paidíon, “boy, lad”), from παῖς (paîs, “child”); some sources consider this unlikely and suggest instead Latin pagus (“countryside”), in sense of "boy f
From Middle Dutch palefroot, from Old French palefroid, from Late Latin paraverēdus. Doublet of paard.
From Middle Dutch palais, from Old French palais, from Latin palātium. Doublet of palts.

parole.significato: a coach attendant, a servant and driver of a carriage
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch palfrenier, from Old French palefrenier, likely from Old Occitan palafrenier, from Latin palafrenārius, from paraveredārius.
From Middle Dutch paneel, from Old French panel, from Medieval Latin pannellus, later variant of pannulus, diminutive of pannus.

parole.significato: parrot, member of the order Psittaciformes, especially of the families Psittacidae and Psittaculidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch papegay, from Old French papegai, ultimately from Arabic ببغاء, of onomatopoeic origin. Cf. English popinjay.

parole.significato: paper (A material used for writing or printing on, made from cellulose pulp rolled into thin sheets.)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch papier, from Old French papier. Doublet of paper.
From Middle Dutch parabel, from Old French parable, parabole, from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison”). Doublet of parabool, palaver, and parool.
From Middle Dutch parament, from Old French parament, from Medieval Latin parāmentum.
From Middle Dutch parlement, from Old French parlement.
From Middle Dutch partie, from Old French partie. Doublet of party.
Deverbal from passen, from Middle Dutch passen, from pas, from Old French pas, from Latin passus. Equivalent to a derivation from etymology 2.

parole.significato: pace, step; also as a measure of distance
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pas, from Old French pas, from Latin passus.

From Middle Dutch passie, from Old French passion, from Latin passiō (“suffering”), noun of action from perfect passive participle passus (“suffered”), from deponent verb patior (“to suffer”), from Proto-Indo-European *pe(i)- (“to hurt”), see also Old English feond (“devil, enemy”), Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌹𐌰𐌽 (fa
From Middle Dutch pateen, patene, from Old French [Term?], from Latin patena, by-form of patina. Doublet of pan and patina.

parole.significato: A partridge, any bird of the genera Perdix or Alectoris.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch patrise, from older partrise, from Old French pertriz, variant of perdriz, from Latin perdīx (“partridge”), from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix, “partridge”). Forms retaining the first r existed into the 17th century.
From Middle Dutch patroon, from Old French patron (“model”), from Latin patrōnus.

From Middle Dutch paus, paues, pauwes, from Old French papes (compare German Papst), from Medieval Latin pāpa (“bishop, pope”), from Ancient Greek πάπας (pápas, “bishop”), variant of πάππας (páppas, “father”), of imitative origin. Doublet of paap.

parole.significato: pewter; originally an alloy of tin and lead, now often tin alloyed with other metals
parole.testo: Ultimately from Old French piautre.
From Middle Dutch pensen, peinsen, from Old French penser, from Latin pensō.
From Middle Dutch pais, borrowed from Old French pais, from Latin pax, from Proto-Italic *pāks, from Proto-Indo-European *péh₂ḱ-s (“peace”). Cognate to English peace and French paix.
From Middle Dutch pelgrimage, from Old French pelerinage (“pilgrimage”). Equivalent to pelgrim + -age.

parole.significato: pelican, bird of the family Pelecanidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pellicaen, from Old French pelican, from Latin pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán).

parole.significato: a long feather of a bird
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch penne, from Old French penne, from Latin penna (“feather”), from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”), from *peth₂- (“to rush, fly”), root of *petra-, whence Ancient Greek πτερόν (pterón, “wing”, whence pterosauriër), and also of Sanskrit पत्रम् (patram, “wing,

parole.significato: pier (piece of wall between two frames or openings, such as windows or doors)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch penant, from Old French penant.

parole.significato: pennon (knight's vane or streamer affixed to a lance)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pennoen, from Old French pennon.
From Middle Dutch pense, from Old French panse (“belly; tripe”), from Latin pantex (“belly; guts”). Cognate with Limburgish pans, West Flemish pense, English paunch.

parole.significato: pension (annuity paid regularly as benefit due to a retired employee)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pensioen, recorded since 1362, from Old French pension (“payment, rent”), from Latin pensio (“payment, rent”), from pensus, the past participle of pendere (“to weigh, to pay”).

parole.significato: a parcel of land, a plot
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch perceel, from older parcheel, from Old French parcelle, from Late Latin particella, from Latin particula.

From Middle Dutch percament, from Old French parchemin, via Latin pergamīna, from Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós, “of Pergamun”), which is named for the Ancient city of Pergamon (modern Bergama) in Asia Minor, where it was invented as an expensive alternative for papyrus.

parole.significato: a burnet, any plant of the genus Sanguisorba
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pimpernelle, from Old French piprenelle, from Medieval Latin pimpinella. Doublet of bevernel.
From Middle Dutch pinakel, from Old French pinacle, from Latin pinnāculum.

parole.significato: a peony, a plant of the genus Paeonia
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pionie, from Old French pyoine, from Latin paeōnia, from Ancient Greek παιωνία (paiōnía).
From Middle Dutch plate, from Old French plate.
From Middle Dutch plāetse, from Old French place.
From Middle Dutch pladijs, from Old Dutch *pladīs, from Old French pladisse, plaïse, plaise, from Latin platessa. Cognate with German Platteis, English plaice.
From Middle Dutch planete, from Old French planete, from Late Latin planēta, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer”).

parole.significato: to plant, place a seed or plant in suitably fertile substrate in order that it may live and grow
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch planten, from Old Dutch planton, from Old French planter, from Latin plantō.
From Middle Dutch plat, from Old French plat, from Vulgar Latin *plattus.
From earlier paveien, altered (possibly influenced by plavuis) from Middle Dutch paveyen, from pavei (“tile”), from Old French [Term?].

From Old French plain, from Latin plānum (“level ground, a plain”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Its use for "square" is an innovation, replacing Middle Dutch plaetse in standard language (compare dialectal plaats). Compare English plain, plane, Portuguese chão, Spanish llano.
From Middle Dutch plaester, from Old French plastre, from Latin plastrum, from emplastrum, from Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρον (émplastron), from ἔμπλαστον (émplaston).

parole.significato: to interrupt a journey, take a rest, make a stop, notably to tend to the needs of traveler(s), vehicle(s), staff and/or…
parole.testo: From peisteren, from Old French paistre (whence French paître) from Latin pascō (“to graze”). The l-sound may be added by influence of etymology 1.

parole.significato: to plead, to argue; to act as attorney in court
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pleiten, from Old French plaider, with t under influence of the noun pleit (modern pleit).

parole.significato: plover, certain waders of the family Charadriidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pluvier, from Old French plovier.
From Middle Dutch plaisant, from Old French plaisant.

parole.significato: to remove flowering side branches (from the main stem) from
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *plûsen (attested in ûteplûsen). Cognate with Middle Low German plûsen (whence ultimately German plustern). Further origin uncertain. Possibly from Old French peluchier.
From Middle Dutch poeder, from Old French poudre, from Latin pulvis. Doublet of pulver (“powder”) and poer (“gunpowder”).

parole.significato: the pile (upstanding usually fine hair) on certain fabrics, velvet or carpeting
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pool, from Old French poil, from Latin pilus (“hair”). Cognate with English pile.

parole.significato: undefined period of time, an indefinite period
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pose, from Old French pose, from Latin pausa. Doublet of pauze and pausa.

parole.significato: a poplar, tree of the genus Populus
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch popelier, from Old French poplier, from Latin pōpulus. The spelling was adapted to the Latin in the seventeenth century.
From Middle Dutch portier, from Old French portier, from Late Latin portārius.
From Middle Dutch pover, from Old French povre, from Latin pauper. Cognate to French pauvre.
From Middle Dutch practike, from Old French practique, from Latin prāctica, from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτική (prāktikḗ).

parole.significato: to carry out, to perform, to bring into practice
parole.testo: Ultimately from Old French practiser.
From Old French predestination, from Late Latin praedestinatio.

parole.significato: leek (a stem vegetable, Allium ampeloprasum syn. Allium porrum)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch poreye, from Old French poree.
From Middle Dutch preus, also prues, pruets, from Old French preux, proz, from Latin prōdest (“it is useful”).
From Middle Dutch prayeel (“lawn, garden, overgrown seat”), from Old French präel (“enclosed pasture”), derived from Old French pred (“meadow”), from Latin prātum (“meadow”).
From Middle Dutch prijs, prise, from Old French pris, preis, from Latin pretium (“worth, price, money spent, wages, reward”).
From Middle Dutch prisen, from Old French priser, from Latin pretiō.
From Middle Dutch primaet, from Old French primat, from Latin prīmātus or Latin prīmus.
From Middle Dutch principael, from Old French principal, from Latin prīncipālis.

From Middle Dutch prince, from Old French prince, from Latin princeps (“first”), notably in princeps civitatis (“first citizen”), the primary title of the Roman 'emperor' under the still republican constitution.
From Old French priorité, from Latin prioritas.
From Middle Dutch prisoen, from Old French prison.
From Middle Dutch privilegie, from Old French privilege, from Latin privilegium.
From Middle Dutch proces, from Old French procés (“journey”), from Latin processus, past participle of procedo.
From Middle Dutch proeve, prueve, from Old French prueve. Equivalent to a deverbal from proeven.

parole.significato: prophet, a messenger chosen by God
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch prophete, from Old French prophete, from Latin propheta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “one who speaks for a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”).
From Middle Dutch prophecie, from Old French prophetie, from Latin prophētīa, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía). By surface analysis, profeet + -ie.
From Middle Dutch profijt, from Old French profit, from Latin profectus.

parole.significato: prolongation, lengthening (especially the extension of a bank loan)
parole.testo: From prolongeren + -atie, from Old French prolongation, from Latin prōlongātiō, from prōlongātus, perfect passive participle of prōlongō, from prō + longus.
From Old French, from Latin prologus, from Ancient Greek πρόλογος (prólogos).
From Middle Dutch prooye, from Old French proie, from Latin praeda.
From Middle Dutch proost, from provest, from Old French provost.
From Middle Dutch proper, from Old French propre, from Latin proprius.
From Old French provocacion, from Latin provocātiō. By surface analysis, provoceren + -atie.

Borrowed from Old French puberté, from Latin pubertas (“the age of maturity, manhood”), from pubes, puber (“grown up, of mature age, adult; of plants, downy, pubescent”). By surface analysis, puber + -teit.
From Middle Dutch poye, from Old French poie, from Latin podia, plural of podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “base”), a diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of podium.
From Middle Dutch pupille, from Old French pupille, from Latin pūpilla.
From Middle Dutch puur, from Old French pur, from Latin pūrus.
From Middle Dutch queste, from Old French queste, from Latin quaesta, from quaesita, from quaesitus. Doublet with queste.
From Middle Dutch rampeneren, ramponeren from Old French ramposner.
From Middle Dutch rantsoen, ransoen, rasoen, from Old French raençon, from Latin redēmptiō, redēmptiōnem. Doublet of redemptie.

From Middle Dutch rebel, from Old French rebelle, from Latin rebellis (“waging war again; insurgent”), from rebellō (“to wage war again, fight back”), from re- (“again, back”) + bellō (“to wage war”).
From Middle Dutch recepte, from Old French recepte, from Medieval Latin recepta.

parole.significato: a register, an index, esp. as an appendix in a book
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch register, from Old French registre, from Medieval Latin registrum, which see.
From Middle Dutch registreren, from Old French registrer, regestrer. By surface analysis, register + -eren.
From Old French, from Latin reliquiae (“remains, relics”), from relinquō (“to leave behind, abandon, relinquish”), from re- + linquō (“to leave, quit, forsake, depart from”).

parole.significato: faith, religion, a system of beliefs dealing with soul, deity and/or life after death
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch religie, earlier also religioen, from Old French religion, from Latin religiō.
From Old French, from Latin reliquiae (“remains, relics”), from relinquō (“to leave behind, abandon, relinquish”), from re- + linquō (“to leave, quit, forsake, depart from”).
From Middle Dutch rente, from Old French rente; cognate with Icelandic renta and Danish rente.
From Middle Dutch representeren, from Old French representer. By surface analysis, re- + presenteren
From Middle Dutch reserveren, from Old French reserver, from Latin reservō.
From Middle Dutch respijt, from Old French respit. Doublet of respect.
From Middle Dutch rieme, from Old French raime.
From Middle Dutch rijm, rīme, from Old French rime, of uncertain origin. More at rhyme.
From Middle Dutch rijs, from Old French ris, from Old Italian riso, risi, from Byzantine Greek ὄρυζα (óruza).
From Middle Dutch riviere, from Old French riviere.

parole.significato: role, function (as in actions or tasks that a person or a group is expected to perform)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rolle, from Old French role.
From Middle Dutch rollen, from Old French roeler.
From Middle Dutch romein, from Old French Romain, from Latin rōmānus.
From Middle Dutch ront, from Old French reont, from Latin rotundus.
From Middle Dutch roye, from Old French roie; more at French raie.

parole.significato: rose, ornamental plant of the genus Rosa
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rose, from Old French rose, from Latin rosa. Doublet of roze.
From Middle Dutch rotse, from Old French roche. Doublet of rock.
From Middle Dutch rosine, from Old French *roisine (“grape”), from Latin racēmus. Cognate with Persian رز (raz, “vine”).
From Middle Dutch rubrike (“red pigment”), from Old French rubrique, from Latin rubrīca (“red ochre”), the substance used to make red letters, from ruber (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.
From Middle Dutch ruter, from Old French routier.
From Middle Dutch rumoer, from Old French rumor, from Latin rumor (“noise”).
From Middle Dutch ruwaert, from dialectal Old French rewart, variant of regart (“overseer”).
From Middle Dutch saye, saey, from Old French saie, from Latin sagum.
From Old French sacrament, from Ecclesiastical Latin sacrāmentum (“sacrament”), from Latin sacrō (“hallow, consecrate”), from sacer (“sacred, holy”), originally sum deposited by parties to a suit.
From Middle Dutch salarijs, from Old French salaire, from Latin salarium (“salt money, money to buy salt with”), from sal (“salt”).

parole.significato: sauce (liquid condiment, usually of more than watery consistency)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sause, from Old French sauce, from Latin salsus (“salt”).
From Middle Dutch schaec, from Old French escac or directly from Medieval Latin scaccus, from Arabic شَاه (šāh), from Classical Persian شاه (šāh, “king”). Doublet of echec.
From Old French eschec mat, from Persian شاه مات (“šâh mât, the king is dead”).

Back-formation from geschakeerd (which was interpreted as a past participle), from Middle Dutch gescakiert, originally a heraldic term (English chequy) referring to checkered squares borrowed from Old French eschequeré.
From Middle Dutch schalie, from Old French escaille.

From Old French escarlate (12c., modern écarlate), from Medieval Latin scarlatum (“scarlet, cloth of scarlet”), from Persian سقرلات (saqerlât, “a kind of rich cloth”), a variant of Arabic سِقِلَّات (siqillāt, “scarlet cloth, rich cloth”), of unknown origin (probably ultimately Persian).

parole.significato: a scaffold where public executions or less commonly corporal punishment or other humiliating punishments took place
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schavot, from Old French eschafaud. Cognate with English scaffold.
From Middle Dutch schofut, scuvut (“eagle owl”). Possibly borrowed from Old French çuete (French chouette).
From Middle Dutch schermutselinge, from the verb schermutsen, from Old French escarmucher.
From Middle Dutch scholier, from Old French escolier, from Latin scholāris. Equivalent to school + -ier.

parole.significato: a scorpion, an arachnid with a venomous sting of the order Scorpiones
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch scorpioen, from Old French scorpion, from Latin scorpiō, from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos).
From Middle Dutch scorce, from Old French escorce (modern écorce), itself from Medieval Latin scorcia, from Latin scortea.

parole.significato: to suspend, delay (an event, proceeding) by inserting a pause
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schorsen, from Old French escorcier, from Vulgar Latin *excurtiō.
From Middle Dutch schuren, probably from Old French escurer. More at English scour, a borrowing from Middle Dutch.
From Old French [Term?], from Latin sculptūra (“sculpture”), from sculpō (“to cut out, to carve in stone”).
From Old French [Term?], from Latin sectio (“cutting, cutting off, excision, amputation of diseased parts of the body, etc.”), from sectus, past participle of secō (“to cut”).
From Old French seigne, a northern variant of signe, from Latin signum. Doublet of zegen.

parole.significato: a season, major part of the year
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch saisoene, sysoen, from Old French saison, from Latin satiōnem.

parole.significato: cult (socially proscribed and often novel religious group)
parole.testo: From Old French secte (“a sect in philosophy or religion”), from Late Latin secta (“a sect in philosophy or religion, a school, party, faction, class, gild, band, particularly a heretical doctrine or sect, etc.”), possibly, from Latin sequi (“to follow”)
From Old French senat, from Latin senātus (“council of elders; a senate”), from senex (“old”).

parole.significato: a serf (semifree peasant obliged to remain on the lord's land and to perform extensive chores for him)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch serf, from Old French serf, from Latin servus.

parole.significato: sergeant (non-commissioned officer in several armed forces)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch seriant, from Old French sergent, from Latin serviēns. The current spelling is influenced by English sergeant.
From Middle Dutch sermoon, borrowed from Old French sermon, from Latin sermō.
From Middle Dutch serpent, from Old French serpent (“snake, serpent”), from Latin serpēns (“snake”), from the verb serpō (“to creep, crawl”).
From Middle Dutch siere, ciere, chiere, from Old French chiere, from Late Latin cara.
From Middle Dutch signieren, which was borrowed from Old French signier (and adapted using the Dutch verbal suffix -eren), but with its spelling re-borrowed from modern French signer.
From Middle Dutch simpel, from Old French simple, from Latin simplus.

parole.significato: a body of water surrounding the inner portion of a city or a village
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch singele, with the sense of a moat, from Old French sengle, cengle (“fence”), from Latin cingulum (“belt”). Doublet of cingel.
From Middle Dutch sent, from Old French seint, from Latin sanctus.

parole.significato: a siren, a noisy warning device
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sirena, serene, from Old French sereine, from Late Latin sirēna, Latin Sīrēn, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). The sense “warning device” derives from French sirène.

From Middle Dutch siroop, from Old French sirop, from Medieval Latin siruppus, syrupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”). Related to sorbet, sherbet. Compare French sirop, Italian siroppo, Spanish jarabe, jarope, Portuguese xarope
From Middle Dutch sober, from Old French sobre, from Latin sōbrius. Doublet of zuiver.
From Middle Dutch solas, solaes, soelaes, from Old French solaz, solas, from Latin sōlācium.
From Middle Dutch soverein, from Old French soverain. Influenced in the first vowel by Middle French souverain and French souverain.

From Middle Dutch souderen, from Old French souder, from Latin solidō. From Middle Dutch somme, borrowed from Old French somme, from Latin summa.
From Middle Dutch spasme, from Old French (e)spasme, from Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós).
From Middle Dutch specerie, from Old French espicerie. Compare English spicery.
From Middle Dutch speciael, from Old French special, from Latin speciālis.
From Old French specifique, from Late Latin specificus (“specific, particular”), from Latin speciēs (“kind”) + faciō (“make”).

parole.significato: to speculate, to imagine, to guess
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch speculeren, from Old French speculer, from Latin speculārī.
From Old French spectacle, from Latin spectaculum (“a show, spectacle”), from spectare (“to see, behold”), frequentative of specere (“to see”). See species.

From Middle Dutch spelonke, from Old French spelonque, from Italian spelonca, from Latin spelunca (“cave, cavern; grotto; den”), from Ancient Greek σπῆλυγξ (spêlunx, “cave”), from Ancient Greek σπέος (spéos, “cave, cavern”).

From Middle Dutch despijt, from Old French despit (from which also English despite), from Latin despectus (“looking down on”). The first syllable de- was later rebracketed and interpreted as a definite article ("de spijt") and was then dropped.
From Middle Dutch spinagie, from Old French espinache, from Latin spinachium, Old Spanish espinaca, from Arabic إسفاناخ, from Persian اسفناج.
From Middle Dutch sponge, from Old French espoinge, from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), from σπόγγος (spóngos), a substrate word.
From Middle Dutch stael, from Old French estal, from Frankish *stalō, *stalu, from Proto-Germanic *staluz (“post, rod, staff; trunk, stump, tail”). See also steel.

From Middle Dutch stampie, itself borrowed from Old French estampie (“noise, commotion; kind of dance”), from the verb estampir (“to stamp the feet”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *stampijan (“to stamp”). Doublet of estampie.
From Middle Dutch standaert, from Old French estandart.

parole.significato: statute, legislation, regulation; written collection of laws or rules
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch statute, from Old French statut, from Latin statūtum.

From Middle Dutch stellage, stellagie, modified (as if from stellen + -age) from stallage, stallaetse (attested from the 13th century), from Old French estalage, from Medieval Latin stallagium. Doublet of etalage.

From late Middle Dutch stēvele, from Old French estivel. Borrowing from Standard German Stiefel (as sometimes assumed) is unlikely for phonetic reasons, but it could well have passed through Low and Central German dialects (Middle High German stivel, Middle Low German stēvel).
From Middle Dutch stiel, from Old French estile. Doublet with stijl.
From Middle Dutch stijl, from Old French estile, from Latin stilus.
From Middle Dutch stoffe, from Old French estophe, estoffe, from estoffer, from Old High German stoffōn. Compare German Stoff, English stuff. Doublet of native stoppen.
From Middle Dutch stofferen, from Old French estoffer, from Old High German stoffōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn. Doublet of stoppen.

parole.significato: course fabric used as a base for embroidery
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stramijn, stamijn, from Old French estamin, estamine (“light wool”), borrowed from Latin stāmineus (“full of threads, fibrous”), from stāmen (“thread”).
From Middle Dutch strop, probably borrowed via Old French estrope (“snare”) from Medieval Latin stroppus, stropus (“band, strap”).
From Middle Dutch struweel, struwelle, strevel, from Old French struvel.

From Middle Dutch substantie, perhaps via Old French substance, in any event from Latin substantia (“substance, essence”), from substāns, present active participle of substō (“exist; literally, stand under”), from sub + stō (“stand”).
From Middle Dutch subtijl, from Old French subtil, from Latin subtīlis, from sub- + tēla (“a web”).

Inherited from Middle Dutch suicker, borrowed from Old French çucre, borrowed from Old Italian zucchero, borrowed from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), borrowed from Middle Persian 𐭱𐭪𐭥 (šakar), borrowed from Gandhari 𐨭𐨐𐨪 (śakara), from Sanskrit शर्क॑रा (śárkarā), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *śárkaraH, from Proto-I

From Old French surpeliz, from Medieval Latin superpelliceum, from Latin super (“over”) and pellis (“fur”).
From Middle Dutch sinagoge, from Old French synagoge, from Latin synagōga, from Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ, “assembly, gathering”).

parole.significato: a pie, large cake, or cobbler
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch tāerte, from Old French tarte.
From Middle Dutch taxe, from Old French taxe, from Latin taxa.
From Middle Dutch talent, from Old French talent, from Latin talentum, from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “a particular weight, balance”), from Proto-Indo-European *tl̥h₂ent-, from *telh₂-.
From Middle Dutch tamboere (“drum”), from Old French tambour. The sense “military-style drummer” came from Middle French tambour.

parole.significato: carpet (a fabric used as a floor covering)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch tapijt, from Old French tapiz.

parole.significato: to feel with the hands, to grope
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch tasten, from Old French taster, from Vulgar Latin taxitō.
From Middle Dutch taxeren, borrowed from Old French taxer.
From Middle Dutch tempeest, from Old French tempeste, from Latin tempestas.
From Middle Dutch tempelier, templier, from Old French templier.
From Middle Dutch tente, from Old French tente, from Vulgar Latin *tenta or *tenda.

parole.significato: term; a word or phrase, especially one from a specialised area of knowledge
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch term, from Old French terme, from Latin terminus.

parole.significato: the volatile essential oil turpentine naturally occurring in certain tree resins
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch terbentijn, also terpentijn, tarpentijn, from Old French terbentine, from Latin terebinthīna (rēsīna), from the tree terebinthus, from Ancient Greek τερέβινθος (terébinthos).

parole.significato: a test, an earthen bowl or pot
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch test, from Old French test, from Latin testum, from testa.

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch testament, derived from Old French testament, derived from Latin testāmentum (“the publication of a will, a will, testament”).
From Middle Dutch tetrarchie, from Old French tetrarchie, from Latin tetrarchia, from Ancient Greek τετραρχίᾱ (tetrarkhíā).
From Middle Dutch tiger, from Old French tigre, from Latin tigris.
From Middle Dutch toer, from Old French tour. Several senses are borrowed from French tour.
From Middle Dutch tornooy, from Old French tornoi. Subsequently probably influenced by French tournoi (“tournament”).
From Middle Dutch tombe, from Old French tombe, from Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).

parole.significato: stage, scene, place for a performance in front of an assembled audience
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch tineel, from Old French tinel; further origin uncertain. The modern Dutch term was adapted to tonen by folk etymology.
Inherited from Middle Dutch tonijn, borrowed from Old French tonine, from Vulgar Latin *thunnīna.

parole.significato: torch (stick with flame at one end)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch tortse, from Old French torche, ultimately from Latin torqueō (“twist”).
From Middle Dutch torre, from Old Dutch turn, from Old French tur, from Latin turris.

parole.significato: to carry or bear with difficulty
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch torsen (“to pack, load”) (compare metathesized trossen, meaning the same), from Old French torser (“to pack, bind together”) (French trousser), from Vulgar Latin *torsare, from *torsus, a variant form of tortus, the past participle of torqueō.

From Old French tragedie, from Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía, “epic play, tragedy”), from τράγος (trágos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”), a reference to the goat-satyrs of the theatrical plays of the Dorians.
From Middle Dutch tripe, from Old French tripe.

From Middle Dutch [Term?], from Old French triomphe, from Latin triumphus (“triumphal procession”), from Old Latin triumpus, from Etruscan *𐌈𐌓𐌉𐌀𐌌𐌐𐌄 (*θriampe), from Ancient Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos, “thriambus”).

parole.significato: group of people or animals (such as a pride of lions or a herd of cows)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch trop, from Old French [Term?], from Medieval Latin troppus. The vowel changed under the influence of Middle French troupe, from Old French trope, from the same Latin word. Further etymology uncertain, but it is often thought to be a borrowing from Old Frankish.

From Middle Dutch trompet, from Old French trompette (“trumpet”), diminutive of trompe (“horn, trump, trumpet”), from Frankish *trumpa, *trumba (“trumpet”). Akin to Old High German trumpa, trumba (“horn, trumpet”), Middle Dutch tromme (“drum”), Middle Low German trumme (“drum”).
From Middle Dutch tronc (“trunk”), from Old French tronc (“trunk”), from Latin truncus (“trunk”).
From Middle Dutch trone, from Old French trone, from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “seat, throne”).
From Middle Dutch [Term?], from Old French truffe, which ultimately derives from Latin tuber.
From Old French tumour, from Latin tumor (“swelling”), from tumeō (“to bulge, swell”).
From Middle Dutch tumult, from Old French tumulte, from Latin tumultus.
From a reinterpretation as a plural of Middle Dutch uyen, from Old French oignon (whence also Southern Dutch ajuin), from Latin ūniō.

parole.significato: university, (university) college (especially in the United States)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch universiteit, from Old French universitei, from Medieval Latin ūniversitās. Compare German Universität.
From Middle Dutch urine, from older orine, from Old French orine, urine, from Latin urina.
From Old French vair, veir, from the accusative singular masculine form of Latin varius (“variegated”).
From Middle Dutch valsch, from Old French fals, from Latin falsus.
From Middle Dutch varieren, borrowed from Old French varier, from Latin variāre.
From Middle Dutch vassael, vasal, from Old French vassal.
Borrowed from Old French venim, from Latin venēnum.
From ver- + brijzelen. Brijzelen comes from Middle Dutch briselen (“to break”), alternative form of brisen, from Old French briser, brisier.
From Middle Dutch vernis, from Old French vernis.
From Middle Dutch vijs, vijse, vise, from Old French vis (“screw”).
From Middle Dutch viver, from Old French vivier, from Latin vīvārium. Was merged with or replaced Middle Dutch wier, wuwer, *wiwer, an older borrowing directly from Latin; compare German Weiher.
From Middle Dutch vilein, from Old French vilain~vilein~villein, from Late Latin vīllānus (“farm worker”), from Latin vīlla.

parole.significato: any violet, an ornamental fragrant plant of the genus Viola (including the pansy)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch viole, older violette, from Old French violette, from viole, from Latin viola.

parole.significato: vision (something dreamlike or imaginary thought to be seen; mystical experience)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch visioen, from Old French vision, from Latin visio (“vision, seeing”), noun of action from the perfect passive participle visus (“that which is seen”), from videre (“to see”, verb) + -io (action noun suffix).
From Middle Dutch visse (“polecat”), borrowed via Old French from Latin vissio (“weasel”) (see French vison (“mink”)). Cognate to English fitchew, English fitch and English fitchet.
From Middle Dutch vitriool, from Old French vitriol, from Latin vitriolum.

parole.significato: visor, a removable protective guard on a (knight's) helmet
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch visiere, from Old French visiere.
From Middle Dutch vlamme, from Old Dutch flamma, from Old French flamme, from Latin flamma.
From Middle Dutch vonte, from Old French fonte, from Latin fons (“source; baptismal font”).
From Middle Dutch vois, from Old French voiz, from Latin vōx.
From Middle Dutch vorme, from Old French forme, from Latin forma (“shape, figure, image, outline, plan, mold, frame, case, etc., manner, sort, kind, etc.”).

parole.significato: midwife (woman who assists women in childbirth)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vroedvrouw, a calque of Old French sage-femme. By surface analysis, vroed (“wise”) + vrouw (“woman”).
From Old French wambais, ultimately probably derived from Proto-Germanic *wambō (“stomach”), whence also wam (“belly”). See German Wams for more.
From Middle Dutch warande, from Old French garande, from garer (“to protect”). Unrelated to veranda, despite by-forms of that word with initial w-.

From Middle Dutch sot, a borrowing from Old French sot, from Medieval Latin sottus, of unknown origin. Possibly an expressive interjection, similar to modern French zut! (“damn it!”). Compare Old English sott (“foolish, stupid”), English sot, modern French sot.
From Middle Dutch siwe; possibly related to Old French suer (“to dry”), from Latin sūgere (“to suck”).

From Middle Dutch amandel, either from Old French amandele or Medieval Latin amandola, both from Late Latin amandula, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē). Cognate to English almond.

parole.significato: etymology (study of the origin and development of words)
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Middle French étymologie (from Old French ethimologie, from Latin) or directly a learned borrowing from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología).
From Middle Dutch hanteren, hantieren, from Old French hanter, via Old Norse (or possibly Old English) from Proto-Germanic *haimatjaną.

From Late Middle Dutch hola (“wait up!, hold on!, calm down!”), which also had the dialectal form holla; compare Middle Low German hola!, holda! (interjection), Middle High German holā! From Middle Dutch olm, from Old Dutch (only attested in toponyms), from Old French olme, from Latin ulmus. Alternatively, inherited from Proto-Germanic *elmaz.
From Middle Dutch pellen. Either derived in Middle Dutch from pelle (“peel, shell”), or borrowed from Old French peler (“to peel”), both ultimately from Old French pel (“skin”).

Borrowed from Middle French pyramide, from Old French piramide, from Latin pȳramis, from Ancient Greek πῡραμίς (pūramís), possibly from πῡρός (pūrós, “wheat”) + ἀμάω (amáō, “reap”) or from Egyptian pr-m-ws.

parole.significato: a sage, herb of the genus Salvia
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch salie, from older saelge, either from Old French selge or from Old Dutch *salviga, from Proto-West Germanic *salbejā.

parole.significato: a narrow sausage made of spiced mince
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *salcijs (attested in the plural as salcijsken), ultimately from Late Latin salsīcia, either directly or- more likely- via Old French salcice. The modern form with /ɑu̯~oː/ appears to have been influenced by later French saucisse.

From Middle Dutch seneschal, seneschael, either via Old French seneschal or directly from Latin siniscalcus, from Proto-Germanic *siniz (“old”) + *skalkaz (“knight, servant”), with its final element being influenced by its cognate native Dutch schalk.

From Middle Dutch souter (which existed alongside forms such as psalter and seltre), possibly with L-vocalization from Old Dutch psaltere, psaltare, from Latin psalterium (possibly by way of a Proto-West Germanic *psalterī), ultimately from Ancient Greek ψᾰλτήρῐον (psăltḗrĭon).
